devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us.
2 Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
3 Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.
devotions.application:
The race in Hebrews is not a sprint. It is the long stretch: the job that stays the same year after year, the child who still struggles, the aging parent who asks the same question for the third time in an hour. The writer expects that we will be tempted to “grow weary and lose heart,” and so offers three helps. First, you are not alone. A “great cloud of witnesses” surrounds you. These are people who trusted God before you and finished their race, perhaps including someone whose faith you watched up close. Second, travel lighter. Some things weigh us down without being wrong. They are just heavy, like an old regret or a need to be seen. And some sin tangles our feet before we realize it.

Third, and most of all, look at Jesus. He did not avoid hardship. He endured the cross, scorning its shame, and He did it for the joy set before Him. He is the one who began your faith and will bring it to completion. When your strength fades, you don’t have to summon more grit. You can consider Him, and let His endurance steady your own.
devotions.question: What is one weight you could set down this week, and what might change if you kept your eyes on Jesus instead?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 A Psalm of thanksgiving. Make a joyful noise to the LORD, all the earth.
2 Serve the LORD with gladness; come into His presence with joyful songs.
3 Know that the LORD is God. It is He who made us, and we are His; we are His people, and the sheep of His pasture.
4 Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise; give thanks to Him and bless His name.
5 For the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever; His faithfulness continues to all generations.
devotions.application:
Psalm 100 doesn’t wait for a good mood. It invites all the earth to make a joyful noise, and then gives the reason in verse 3: the Lord made us, and we are His. Before you are an employee, a parent, a caregiver, or anything else, you belong to Someone. You are a sheep in His pasture, known and kept.

That can change how an ordinary day feels. Serving the Lord with gladness might look like cooking dinner for people who won’t say thank you, or bringing patience to a hard conversation. Entering His gates with thanksgiving can start small: naming three ordinary gifts before the day gets busy, or pausing in a parked car to thank Him for the person who tests your patience most. Gratitude isn’t pretending life is easy. It rests on verse 5: “the LORD is good, and His loving devotion endures forever.” His faithfulness reaches to all generations, including yours and the people you love. Whatever comes, you walk into it as one of His.
devotions.question: Who in your life could you serve with gladness this week, remembering that you, and they, belong to the Lord as sheep of His pasture?

devotions.scriptureBody:
11 While Jesus was on His way to Jerusalem, He was passing between Samaria and Galilee.
12 As He entered one of the villages, He was met by ten lepers. They stood at a distance
13 and raised their voices, shouting, “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!”
14 When Jesus saw them, He said, “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” And as they were on their way, they were cleansed.
15 When one of them saw that he was healed, he came back, praising God in a loud voice.
16 He fell facedown at Jesus’ feet in thanksgiving to Him—and he was a Samaritan.
17 “Were not all ten cleansed?” Jesus asked. “Where then are the other nine?
18 Was no one found except this foreigner to return and give glory to God?”
19 Then Jesus said to him, “Rise and go; your faith has made you well!”
devotions.application:
The ten lepers did exactly what Jesus told them. They obeyed, they walked, and somewhere on the road their skin became clean. Nine kept going, probably toward the priests, then home, family, and a life they had been shut out of for years. It is hard to blame them. Only one stopped, turned around, and let his joy be loud. And he was a Samaritan, the outsider, the one nobody expected.

It is easy to be one of the nine. A prayer gets answered, a friend who had stopped calling reaches out again, and we move on to the next worry. The gift is real, but the Giver slips from view. Gratitude often means turning back on purpose: pausing long enough to name what was given and saying thank you out loud. Jesus saw the one who returned, and He spoke a fuller blessing over him: “Rise and go; your faith has made you well!” Being healed was one thing; being met face to face by Jesus was another. There may be a mercy you have already walked past, still close enough to turn back toward.
devotions.question: When you think back over recent days, what good gift have you hurried past, and what would it look like to turn back and thank God?

devotions.scriptureBody:
7 For the LORD your God is bringing you into a good land, a land of brooks and fountains and springs that flow through the valleys and hills;
8 a land of wheat, barley, vines, fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of olive oil and honey;
9 a land where you will eat food without scarcity, where you will lack nothing; a land whose rocks are iron and whose hills are ready to be mined for copper.
10 When you eat and are satisfied, you are to bless the LORD your God for the good land that He has given you.
11 Be careful not to forget the LORD your God by failing to keep His commandments and ordinances and statutes, which I am giving you this day.
12 Otherwise, when you eat and are satisfied, when you build fine houses in which to dwell,
13 and when your herds and flocks grow large and your silver and gold increase and all that you have is multiplied,
14 then your heart will become proud, and you will forget the LORD your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
15 He led you through the vast and terrifying wilderness with its venomous snakes and scorpions, a thirsty and waterless land. He brought you water from the rock of flint.
16 He fed you in the wilderness with manna that your fathers had not known, in order to humble you and test you, so that in the end He might cause you to prosper.
17 You might say in your heart, “The power and strength of my hands have made this wealth for me.”
18 But remember that it is the LORD your God who gives you the power to gain wealth, in order to confirm His covenant that He swore to your fathers even to this day.
devotions.application:
Moses speaks these words before the good days arrive. He knows that hard seasons often keep us close to God, while comfortable ones can pull us away before we feel it happening. That drift rarely comes through dramatic rebellion. It comes through forgetting. A full table, a small business that finally turns a profit, and slowly the story we tell ourselves shifts: I did this. My hands, my effort, my planning. The passage does not scold hard work or call wealth wrong. It asks us to remember.

The same God who brought water from the rock of flint and fed His people with manna is the One who gave you the strength to rise, the mind to do your work, and the people who opened doors along the way. Even your good seasons are part of His faithfulness to His covenant, the binding promise He swore long before you were born. So when you eat and are satisfied, you might pause and bless the Lord before the next bite or the next task. Remembering does not need to be grand. It can be as small as tracing one good thing back to the hand that gave it.
devotions.question: How might remembering God change the way you see one good thing you have worked hard for and are tempted to credit to your own hands?

devotions.scriptureBody:
16 Rejoice at all times.
17 Pray without ceasing.
18 Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.
devotions.application:
These three short lines can sound impossible on an ordinary day. Rejoice at all times, even on the afternoon your child’s fever climbs and every plan for the day falls apart? Look closely at what Paul asks: “Give thanks in every circumstance.” He says in every circumstance, not for every circumstance. You are not asked to call the hard thing good. You are invited to remember, right in the middle of it, that God is still near and still giving.

Praying without ceasing is not about sitting with folded hands all day. It can look like a word under your breath at a red light, a breath of thanks as you rinse a dish, or a whispered “help” before a hard conversation. Over time, these small turnings become a steady conversation running beneath everything else. And Paul says this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus. When you wonder what God wants of you, here is part of the answer, small enough to begin right where you are: one moment of joy received, one prayer offered, one thank-you spoken.
devotions.question: Which circumstance weighing on you right now could become a place to turn toward God with one honest word of thanks?

devotions.scriptureBody:
9 You attend to the earth and water it; with abundance You enrich it. The streams of God are full of water, for You prepare our grain by providing for the earth.
10 You soak its furrows and level its ridges; You soften it with showers and bless its growth.
11 You crown the year with Your bounty, and Your paths overflow with plenty.
12 The pastures of the wilderness overflow; the hills are robed with joy.
13 The pastures are clothed with flocks, and the valleys are decked with grain. They shout in triumph; indeed, they sing.
devotions.application:
This psalm pictures God as a farmer who takes His time. He attends to the earth, soaks its furrows, levels its ridges, and softens the soil with showers. Much of that work happens out of sight, long before anyone sees grain. Some days feel like that hard, ridged soil. Think of a parent sitting across from a teenager who answers every question with a shrug, week after week. It is easy to assume nothing is growing. Yet the psalmist sees God’s care in the slow, ordinary rain, not only in the harvest.

Look, too, where the overflow reaches: “the pastures of the wilderness.” Even the places we would write off as dry and forgotten are not beyond His attention. Looking back over recent months, you may find more bounty than you expected: a meal shared, a friend who called, strength for a hard week. These are not small things; they are His paths overflowing with plenty. Creation answers with a song, the valleys shouting in triumph and the hills robed with joy. Whatever the day holds, you are welcome to let your own heart join them.
devotions.question: Where in your life does the ground feel hard and ridged right now, and what slow, ordinary rain of God’s care might you be overlooking there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
5 When Jesus looked up and saw a large crowd coming toward Him, He said to Philip, “Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?”
6 But He was asking this to test him, for He knew what He was about to do.
7 Philip answered, “Two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread for each of them to have a small piece.”
8 One of His disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to Him,
9 “Here is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?”
10 “Have the people sit down,” Jesus said. Now there was plenty of grass in that place, so the men sat down, about five thousand of them.
11 Then Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted.
12 And when everyone was full, He said to His disciples, “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.”
13 So they collected them and filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the five barley loaves left over by those who had eaten.
devotions.application:
Philip did the math, and the math was honest: two hundred denarii wouldn’t buy even a small piece of bread for each person. Andrew found a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish, then asked, “But what difference will these make among so many?” That arithmetic is familiar. It might be what you can offer a friend whose marriage is coming apart: a meal, an evening, a few clumsy words that feel like nothing against so much hurt.

Jesus already knew what He would do. He didn’t scold Philip’s numbers or Andrew’s doubt. He had the people sit down on the grass, took what was there, gave thanks for it, and gave it out until everyone had as much as they wanted. What you bring may look just as small: an honest hour of work, a short prayer, a tired yes. It was never meant to feed the whole crowd on its own. You can place it in His hands and see what He does with it. And look at the twelve baskets at the end: He even cared about the leftover pieces, so that nothing would be wasted.
devotions.question: What do you have that feels too small to matter right now, and what might change if you placed it in Jesus’ hands with thanks?

devotions.scriptureBody:
6 Remember this: Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.
7 Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver.
8 And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.
9 As it is written: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.”
10 Now He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your store of seed and will increase the harvest of your righteousness.
11 You will be enriched in every way to be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will produce thanksgiving to God.
devotions.application:
There is a familiar tug-of-war that starts when someone asks for help. Part of us wants to give, and part of us does the math and worries about what will be left. Paul doesn't scold that worry. He reminds the Corinthians where the seed came from in the first place. God is the One “who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food.” What we hold was first handed to us, and His hands keep supplying it.

That frees giving from regret and pressure. Paul says each one should give “what he has decided in his heart to give,” not because someone leaned on them. And generosity can reach beyond money. It might be an unhurried hour with a widower down the hall, or a pot of soup carried to a family with a new baby. Look at where Paul says the harvest lands. It isn't in bigger barns. It is in “every good work” and in thanksgiving rising to God from people who were helped. You might watch for one small place where an open hand would come easily, and see what grows.
devotions.question: Who has God placed within reach of your open hand, and what part of the seed He has supplied could you sow toward them gladly?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good. His loving devotion endures forever.
2 Give thanks to the God of gods. His loving devotion endures forever.
3 Give thanks to the Lord of lords. His loving devotion endures forever.
4 He alone does great wonders. His loving devotion endures forever.
5 By His insight He made the heavens. His loving devotion endures forever.
6 He spread out the earth upon the waters. His loving devotion endures forever.
7 He made the great lights—His loving devotion endures forever.
8 the sun to rule the day, His loving devotion endures forever.
9 the moon and stars to govern the night. His loving devotion endures forever.
devotions.application:
Psalm 136 repeats one line in every verse: His loving devotion endures forever. That can feel like a lot, until you think about how a day actually goes. A kind word fades within hours, while a worry or a sharp exchange at home replays again and again. So the psalm answers repetition with repetition. It begins with who God is: good, and above every other power people bow to. Then it turns to what is in plain sight: the sky, the ground under your feet, the sun that rules the day, and the moon and stars that govern the night. Each one comes with the same refrain, as if to say, this, too, is His steady love.

You could borrow the pattern. Pick one small, ordinary thing, like the warmth of a mug in your hands, and add the refrain to it. You may not feel anything dramatic, and that’s all right. God’s faithfulness is often seen one small thing at a time, the way this psalm sees it, verse by verse.
devotions.question: When you look at something ordinary in your day, what changes if you add the words “His loving devotion endures forever” to it?

devotions.scriptureBody:
19 Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break in and steal.
20 But store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy, and where thieves do not break in and steal.
21 For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.
devotions.application:
Few people think of themselves as treasure hunters. Yet watch where your thoughts wander in a spare minute. For one person it’s the kitchen they keep planning to remodel; for another, a savings goal that never feels high enough. Jesus isn’t scolding us for owning things or planning ahead. He’s telling the plain truth about them. Moth and rust get to everything eventually. Paint fades, engines fail, and the jacket we were proud of a few years ago ends up in a yard sale.

Then He points to treasure that lasts: a meal shared with a lonely neighbor, patience with a tired child, money given without fanfare where it’s needed, and unhurried time with God. None of it shows up on a statement, yet nothing can wear it down or carry it off. And look at His closing line: “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” Our hearts follow our treasure, not the other way around. So we don’t have to wait until we feel generous or free of worry. We can begin with one small choice and let our hearts catch up.
devotions.question: How do the places your time, money, and worry went this past week reveal what your heart treasures most?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 Now Naomi had a relative on her husband’s side, a prominent man of noble character from the clan of Elimelech, whose name was Boaz.
2 And Ruth the Moabitess said to Naomi, “Please let me go into the fields and glean heads of grain after someone in whose sight I may find favor.” “Go ahead, my daughter,” Naomi replied.
3 So Ruth departed and went out into the field and gleaned after the harvesters. And she happened to come to the part of the field belonging to Boaz, who was from the clan of Elimelech.
4 Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and said to the harvesters, “The LORD be with you.” “The LORD bless you,” they replied.
5 And Boaz asked the foreman of his harvesters, “Whose young woman is this?”
6 The foreman answered, “She is the Moabitess who returned with Naomi from the land of Moab.
7 She has said, ‘Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the harvesters.’ So she came out and has continued from morning until now, except that she rested a short time in the shelter.”
8 Then Boaz said to Ruth, “Listen, my daughter. Do not go and glean in another field, and do not go away from this place, but stay here close to my servant girls.
9 Let your eyes be on the field they are harvesting, and follow along after these girls. Indeed, I have ordered the young men not to touch you. And when you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the young men have filled.”
10 At this, she fell on her face, bowing low to the ground, and said to him, “Why have I found such favor in your eyes that you should take notice of me, even though I am a foreigner?”
11 Boaz replied, “I have been made fully aware of all you have done for your mother-in-law since the death of your husband, how you left your father and mother and the land of your birth, and how you came to a people you did not know before.
12 May the LORD repay your work, and may you receive a rich reward from the LORD, the God of Israel, under whose wings you have taken refuge.”
devotions.application:
Ruth’s day begins with something small and humbling: asking permission to pick up leftover grain behind someone else’s harvesters. She is a foreigner, a widow, and hungry, with no idea who will treat her kindly. You may know a version of that, perhaps a first shift where no one has learned your name yet. Ruth goes anyway and does the next faithful thing, working steadily from morning on, with only a short rest in the shelter.

Then the story says she “happened to come” to the part of the field belonging to Boaz. It reads like chance, yet the whole book hints that the Lord is at work in the ordinary turns of a day. Boaz protects her and points her to the water jars. He had already heard how she cared for Naomi; her unseen faithfulness had been seen after all. Boaz blesses her as one who has taken refuge under God’s wings, and here those wings look like a generous landowner and a cool drink. Your hidden care for others may matter more than you know. And you might be the one who sees the outsider in your own field and makes room.
devotions.question: Which ordinary place you’ve happened to land might be where the Lord is at work, and who there is waiting for someone to see them?

devotions.scriptureBody:
6 Therefore, just as you have received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to walk in Him,
7 rooted and built up in Him, established in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness.
devotions.application:
Paul doesn’t ask the Colossians to find something new. He asks them to keep going the way they began. The same Jesus you first received as Lord is the One you walk with now, even while you fold laundry and glance at the clock because your teenager is late getting home. Walking is ordinary and slow. It happens one step at a time, mostly unseen.

Paul layers his pictures: roots sunk deep, a building rising course by course, a faith made firm in what you were taught. None of these come together overnight. A wall goes up one stone at a time, each laid on the last. You may feel more scattered than rooted, pulled by a strained friendship or a worry you can’t set down. Paul doesn’t tell you to start over. He urges you to “continue to walk in Him.” The invitation may be to stay near Christ in the small, returning moments. And then comes the surprising mark of a rooted life: “overflowing with thankfulness.” This isn’t forced cheer. It is gratitude for gifts already given, like a shared meal, a kind word, or the fact that someone once taught you this faith at all.
devotions.question: Where do you feel most uprooted right now, and what would it look like to keep walking with Christ right there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 A Psalm. A song for the Sabbath day. It is good to praise the LORD, and to sing praises to Your name, O Most High,
2 to proclaim Your loving devotion in the morning and Your faithfulness at night
3 with the ten-stringed harp and the melody of the lyre.
4 For You, O LORD, have made me glad by Your deeds; I sing for joy at the works of Your hands.
devotions.application:
The psalmist begins plainly: it is good to praise the Lord. Not required, not impressive, just good, the way bread or rest is good. This was a song for the Sabbath, a day set aside to stop working and remember who holds everything together. The psalm moves in a rhythm: His loving devotion in the morning, His faithfulness at night. Morning is when we face what is ahead, perhaps a feverish child on a day already full of plans. It helps to start by naming God’s steady love before the day names its demands. Night is when we look back, and we often count what went wrong. The psalm invites another kind of counting. Where was God faithful? Maybe in a meal shared, a hard conversation that went better than feared, or strength enough for one more task.

The psalmist’s gladness grows from what God has done, “the works of Your hands.” You do not need a harp or a lyre. A whispered thank-you at the breakfast table or a few lines of a song before sleep will do. Praise like this does not ignore trouble. It sets God’s deeds right beside it, so the whole picture comes into view.
devotions.question: What small evidence of the Lord’s faithfulness can you trace in the ordinary hours behind you, and what would it sound like to thank Him for it?

devotions.scriptureBody:
41 As Jesus was sitting opposite the treasury, He watched the crowd putting money into it. And many rich people put in large amounts.
42 Then one poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which amounted to a small fraction of a denarius.
43 Jesus called His disciples to Him and said, “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury.
44 For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”
devotions.application:
Jesus sat across from the treasury and watched. He saw the rich put in large amounts, and He saw a poor widow drop in two small copper coins that the crowd hardly registered. Then He called His disciples to Him, because He wanted them to see what He saw: this woman had given more than all the others. They gave out of their surplus, but she “out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.”

It is easy to feel that what we bring is too small. Think of a grandmother who can no longer cook for the church supper, so she writes one card each week to someone who is grieving, in handwriting that shakes. Next to people who seem to give so much more, an offering like that can look like almost nothing. But Jesus does not measure the way the crowd measures. He sees what a gift costs, not only what it looks like. Whatever you hold in your hand, however small, is seen by the One who saw two copper coins and called them more. Nothing given to Him in trust is too little to matter.
devotions.question: Who in your life receives the small, costly things you give, and how does it change your offering to know Jesus sees what it costs?

devotions.scriptureBody:
20 Then Noah built an altar to the LORD. And taking from every kind of clean animal and clean bird, he offered burnt offerings on the altar.
21 When the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma, He said in His heart, “Never again will I curse the ground because of man, even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth. And never again will I destroy all living creatures as I have done.
22 As long as the earth endures, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall never cease.”
devotions.application:
Noah steps off the ark into a world scrubbed bare. No house, no fields, no neighbors. And the first thing he builds is an altar. Before he plants or plans, he turns toward the Lord. Your own ground may feel bare right now, perhaps after a move to a city where no one yet knows your name. Noah’s worship came first, not after everything was rebuilt.

Then listen to what God says. He knows that “every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth.” The flood did not fix that. Yet He makes His promise anyway. His faithfulness does not wait on our improvement. And He ties that promise to things so ordinary we barely see them: seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night. The sun will rise again whether you slept well or not, whether the day ahead looks hopeful or hard. Each sunrise and each change of season repeats what God said. When your days feel unsteady, the steady turning of the world is more than weather. It is God keeping His word.
devotions.question: When your days feel unsteady, how might ordinary rhythms like morning light, shared meals, and changing seasons remind you that God is still keeping His word?

devotions.scriptureBody:
34 Jesus explained, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.
35 Do you not say, ‘There are still four months until the harvest’? I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest.
36 Already the reaper draws his wages and gathers a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together.
37 For in this case the saying ‘One sows and another reaps’ is true.
38 I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the hard work, and now you have taken up their labor.”
devotions.application:
Jesus speaks of a different kind of food: “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” There is a nourishment that comes from doing what God has put in front of us, even on a thin, tiring day. Like the people Jesus addressed, we tell ourselves the harvest is still months away: someday, when life calms down, when I feel ready. Jesus gently turns our heads and tells us to “lift up your eyes and look at the fields.” The teenager who lingers in the kitchen after dinner, longer than usual, may be closer to the harvest than you think.

There is freedom here too. Jesus says that “others have done the hard work.” Long before you came into someone’s life, others prayed for them, taught them, and loved them. Some days you plant and never see what grows; some days you gather what someone else planted long ago. And Jesus says the sower and the reaper rejoice together. You don’t have to carry the whole harvest. You only have to lift your eyes.
devotions.question: How might Jesus be asking you to lift your eyes, and whose earlier faithfulness are you gathering from without realizing it?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 A song of ascents. When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers.
2 Then our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with shouts of joy. Then it was said among the nations, “The LORD has done great things for them.”
3 The LORD has done great things for us; we are filled with joy.
4 Restore our captives, O LORD, like streams in the Negev.
5 Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy.
6 He who goes out weeping, bearing a trail of seed, will surely return with shouts of joy, carrying sheaves of grain.
devotions.application:
This psalm holds two things at once: a memory of joy and a prayer for more. The people remember when the Lord brought them home. It felt like a dream, and their mouths were filled with laughter. Then, in the very next breath, they pray, “Restore our captives, O LORD.” Even after great things, some places in life still feel dry and waiting.

For you it might be a grown son who has stopped returning your calls, while you keep leaving warm messages anyway. The psalm is honest that this is hard. It pictures someone going out weeping, still carrying seed, still planting. The tears and the sowing happen together. Faithful, ordinary things done with a heavy heart, like making dinner or praying the same prayer again, count as sowing. The streams of the Negev were dry desert channels that could fill quickly when the rains came. What looks empty now can run with water. And the psalm makes a promise: “Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy.” You can hold on to what the Lord has already done for you, and keep scattering seed.
devotions.question: Which seed are you sowing with tears right now, and which of the great things the Lord has already done for you helps you keep planting?

devotions.scriptureBody:
7 Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return.
8 The one who sows to please his flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction; but the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life.
9 Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.
10 Therefore, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith.
devotions.application:
Much of what grows in a life is planted without anyone watching. A patient answer to a tired child. A shortcut at work because no one will check. An hour given to a lonely neighbor, or an evening spent nursing an old grudge. Paul reminds us that none of it is hidden from God, and He is not fooled. Whatever we sow, we reap. That is a warning, but it is also a promise. Small, faithful choices made to please the Spirit do not vanish into nothing.

The hard part is the waiting. Kindness often goes unthanked. Prayer for a struggling friend seems to change little. Being honest with money can feel like falling behind. Paul knows this, which is why he says, “Let us not grow weary in well-doing.” The harvest comes “in due time,” not on our schedule. Meanwhile, each day brings its own chances to do good: to a worn-out cashier, a stranger, or someone in the family of faith who is hurting without saying so. You don’t have to do everything. You can plant what is in front of you.
devotions.question: Where in your ordinary days are you tempted to give up on doing good, and what small seed could you plant there today?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners,
2 to proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor and the day of our God’s vengeance, to comfort all who mourn,
3 to console the mourners in Zion—to give them a crown of beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and a garment of praise for a spirit of despair. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified.
devotions.application:
Some days begin already heavy: a grief we haven’t named, or a conversation with a grown child that went wrong and keeps replaying. Isaiah speaks right into those places. The Lord sends His anointed one not to the strong and put-together, but to the poor, the brokenhearted, the captive, and those who mourn. Jesus later read these words aloud in His hometown and said they were being fulfilled in Him. That means His attention turns first toward whatever in you feels broken or bound.

Look at the exchanges: a crown of beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, a garment of praise for a spirit of despair. He doesn’t ask you to hide the ashes or act as if they aren’t there. He meets you in them and offers something better to wear. And the picture ends with oaks, trees that grow slowly, put down deep roots, and stand through storms. You don’t have to make yourself strong by sheer effort. You are the Lord’s planting. Your growth may be slow and unseen, but it is His work, and He is patient with you.
devotions.question: What ashes are you carrying today, and what might it look like to let the Lord meet you there with His comfort?

devotions.scriptureBody:
22 Then Jesus said to His disciples, “Therefore I tell you, do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear.
23 For life is more than food, and the body more than clothes.
24 Consider the ravens: They do not sow or reap, they have no storehouse or barn; yet God feeds them. How much more valuable you are than the birds!
25 Who of you by worrying can add a single hour to his life?
26 So if you cannot do such a small thing, why do you worry about the rest?
27 Consider how the lilies grow: They do not labor or spin. Yet I tell you, not even Solomon in all his glory was adorned like one of these.
28 If that is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, how much more will He clothe you, O you of little faith!
29 And do not be concerned about what you will eat or drink. Do not worry about it.
30 For the Gentiles of the world strive after all these things, and your Father knows that you need them.
31 But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.
devotions.application:
Jesus doesn't scold His disciples for having needs. He names them plainly: food, clothes, and drink. Then He says something tender: “your Father knows that you need them.” Worry often grows from the feeling that no one else is keeping track. We fear that if we stop turning a problem over at 2 a.m., it will slip through the cracks. Jesus points us outside, to ravens with no storehouse or barn and lilies that never spin a thread. He invites us to look long enough to remember who is holding things together.

This doesn't mean our needs are unimportant. A parent still counts out lunch money for a child's school trip, and Jesus isn't telling us to stop working or planning. But worry can't add a single hour to our lives, and it slowly crowds out the one thing Jesus asks us to seek: His kingdom, His way of doing things, and His care for the people around us. The practice can be small. Watch a bird on a wire for a moment, let it remind you how valuable you are to God, and turn one anxious thought into a prayer before moving on.
devotions.question: Who do you picture keeping track of your needs when worry wakes you, and how might trusting your Father who already knows change what you seek first?

devotions.scriptureBody:
13 Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and Your dominion endures through all generations. The LORD is faithful in all His words and kind in all His actions.
14 The LORD upholds all who fall and lifts up all who are bowed down.
15 The eyes of all look to You, and You give them their food in season.
16 You open Your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing.
17 The LORD is righteous in all His ways and kind in all His deeds.
18 The LORD is near to all who call on Him, to all who call out to Him in truth.
19 He fulfills the desires of those who fear Him; He hears their cry and saves them.
20 The LORD preserves all who love Him, but all the wicked He will destroy.
21 My mouth will declare the praise of the LORD; let every creature bless His holy name forever and ever.
devotions.application:
Look how often the word “all” appears here. The LORD upholds all who fall, lifts up all who are bowed down, and is near to all who call on Him. The welcome is wide. The psalm does speak of those who call on Him in truth, who fear Him and love Him, and it says plainly that “all the wicked He will destroy.” Yet the door it describes is open to anyone who turns toward Him honestly. If you are carrying something heavy, like a strained conversation at home or a body that won’t do what it used to, you can stand among the “all.”

The psalm pictures every living thing looking up, like a household waiting at the table, and God opening His hand. Much of what sustains us arrives without fanfare: a meal, a night’s sleep, a friend’s call at the right moment. This passage invites us to see an open hand behind them. When life feels unsteady, verse 13 holds firm: “Your dominion endures through all generations.” Calling on Him in truth means coming honestly, not with polished words. You can bring Him the real thing, even if it is only a cry. He hears.
devotions.question: When you feel bowed down, what would it look like to call on the Lord in truth, bringing Him the real thing instead of polished words?

devotions.scriptureBody:
31 When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne.
32 All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate the people one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats.
33 He will place the sheep on His right and the goats on His left.
34 Then the King will say to those on His right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.
35 For I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave Me something to drink, I was a stranger and you took Me in,
36 I was naked and you clothed Me, I was sick and you looked after Me, I was in prison and you visited Me.’
37 Then the righteous will answer Him, ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You, or thirsty and give You something to drink?
38 When did we see You a stranger and take You in, or naked and clothe You?
39 When did we see You sick or in prison and visit You?’
40 And the King will reply, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me.’
devotions.application:
The most striking thing in this scene may be the surprise. The people the King welcomes don’t remember seeing Him at all. They remember a meal for a hungry neighbor, a cup of water, a spare room, a coat handed over, an afternoon beside a sickbed, and a visit to someone in prison whom others had written off. To them it was just the next thing that needed doing. Jesus says He was there the whole time.

That changes how an ordinary day looks. Think of the aging parent who calls a little too often, or the family that moved in down the street and still doesn’t know a soul. Christ has tied Himself to people like these and calls them His own family. You don’t need a grand plan or a spotless heart to begin. Small kindness, given without keeping score, does not go unseen by the King before whom all the nations will be gathered. You may meet Him without recognizing Him, and that is all right. The invitation is to keep your eyes and your hands open.
devotions.question: How might one of “the least of these” already be near you, and what small kindness could you offer without keeping score?

devotions.scriptureBody:
15 Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise,
16 redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
17 Therefore do not be foolish, but understand what the Lord’s will is.
18 Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit.
19 Speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Sing and make music in your hearts to the Lord,
20 always giving thanks to God the Father for everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
devotions.application:
Paul doesn’t ask us to walk faster, only more carefully. Days tend to slip by in small pieces, like the half hour after dinner that vanishes before anyone decides what to do with it. “Redeeming the time” suggests those pieces can be bought back. That doesn’t happen by cramming more in. It happens by paying attention to where we’re going and who we’re walking with.

Paul names one familiar way people try to escape a hard day: drinking until the edges blur. We all have our own versions, whatever we reach for to numb rather than to rest. They promise relief and leave us emptier. He offers something better: “be filled with the Spirit,” letting God’s own presence steady us from the inside. That looks surprisingly ordinary. A hymn hummed while folding laundry. A psalm read aloud with a friend who is struggling. Thanks spoken at a crowded table, or whispered in a hospital waiting room. Giving thanks “for everything” isn’t calling loss good. It is trusting that the Father is present even there.
devotions.question: Which small, overlooked moment in your day could you redeem by turning it into thanks to God, and what would that look like?

devotions.scriptureBody:
17 Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow.
18 He chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation.
devotions.application:
Good things often arrive without fanfare: a friend who remembers a hard anniversary and calls, a meal someone else cooked, a child’s laugh from the next room. James says none of these are accidents. “Every good and perfect gift is from above,” coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights. The sun and moon He made rise and set, and shadows stretch and shrink through the day, but God Himself does not shift. His goodness does not rise and fall with your mood, your circumstances, or how well you slept last night.

That steadiness matters most on the days you feel unsteady. James adds that God chose to give us birth through the word of truth. It was His idea and His doing, before you ever reached for Him. And He calls us firstfruits, like the first sheaves of a harvest that promise more is coming. Your life, ordinary as it may feel, is meant to be an early sign of the harvest God intends for all His creation. As you go about your day, you might pick one good gift and trace it back to the Giver.
devotions.question: Where in your life have you started treating a good gift as ordinary, and how might receiving it from God’s unchanging hand change the way you hold it?

devotions.scriptureBody:
12 How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?
13 I will lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD.
14 I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people.
15 Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints.
16 Truly, O LORD, I am Your servant; I am Your servant, the son of Your maidservant; You have broken my bonds.
17 I will offer to You a sacrifice of thanksgiving and call on the name of the LORD.
18 I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people,
19 in the courts of the LORD’s house, in your midst, O Jerusalem. Hallelujah!
devotions.application:
The psalmist asks a question that often rises when a hard season finally lifts: how can I ever repay this? His first move is surprising. Before he offers anything, he lifts the cup of salvation and calls on the name of the Lord. He receives again and leans on God again. Only then does he speak of keeping his vows and bringing a sacrifice of thanksgiving. Gratitude here begins with open hands, not with settling a debt.

His thanks isn’t kept private, either. He keeps his promises “in the presence of all His people.” That might look like telling a friend at dinner what God carried you through, or following through on something you promised Him from a hospital waiting room. Even the hardest things have a place in this psalm. The death of God’s people is precious in His sight, never overlooked. If you are grieving or afraid, that line is for you. You belong to Him, and He has broken your bonds. A sacrifice of thanksgiving may be as small as saying thank you while part of you would rather keep counting what’s wrong.
devotions.question: What has the Lord done for you that you have never said out loud, and who in your life might need to hear you give thanks for it?

devotions.scriptureBody:
10 Then David blessed the LORD in the sight of all the assembly and said: “May You be blessed, O LORD, God of our father Israel, from everlasting to everlasting.
11 Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the splendor and the majesty, for everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You. Yours, O LORD, is the kingdom, and You are exalted as head over all.
12 Both riches and honor come from You, and You are the ruler over all. In Your hands are power and might to exalt and give strength to all.
13 Now therefore, our God, we give You thanks, and we praise Your glorious name.
14 But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.
devotions.application:
David has just watched his people give generously, and his first words are not about how much was given but about whose it all was. He says, “For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You.” It is a humbling way to see what we call ours: a skill your hands learned over many years, the people around your table, even the strength to get out of bed. You still carry these things and care for them, but each one arrived as a gift before it was ever earned.

That changes generosity. Giving stops being a loss we brace for and becomes passing along what was placed in our hands. It changes worry, too. If riches, honor, and strength come from the One who is ruler over all, then a thin month does not decide your future. Some days are full of obvious gifts; others feel lean and ordinary. Either way, David’s wonder fits: who am I, that I should have anything to give? One honest response is to name a few gifts slowly, thank God for them, and hold them a little more loosely.
devotions.question: Who would you become if you held the thing you most call your own as something placed in your hands by God?

devotions.scriptureBody:
25 There will be signs in the sun and moon and stars, and on the earth dismay among the nations, bewildered by the roaring of the sea and the surging of the waves.
26 Men will faint from fear and anxiety over what is coming upon the earth, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
27 At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory.
28 When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.”
devotions.application:
Some seasons feel like the roaring of the sea. Jesus speaks of nations in dismay and of people fainting from fear and anxiety over what is coming upon the earth. He does not wave these things away; He names them plainly. He knows what fear does to us. It narrows our sight until all we can see is the next wave and the next thing that might go wrong.

Yet in exactly those moments, Jesus tells His friends, “stand up and lift up your heads.” The waves are not small, but Someone greater than the waves is coming. The Son of Man arrives “with power and great glory,” and His coming means our redemption, our being set free and brought home to God, “is drawing near.” Lifting our heads is not a trick of willpower. It is turning our attention from what is shaking to the One who is coming. When your own corner of the world trembles, you can look up and remember who is on the way. Fear may still be present, but it does not get to set the direction of your gaze. Christ is nearer than the storm.
devotions.question: When fear pulls your eyes down to the waves, what would it look like to lift your head toward the Son of Man who is coming?

devotions.scriptureBody:
2 In the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills, and all nations will stream to it.
3 And many peoples will come and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob. He will teach us His ways so that we may walk in His paths.” For the law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
4 Then He will judge between the nations and arbitrate for many peoples. They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor train anymore for war.
5 Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the LORD.
devotions.application:
Isaiah’s vision reaches us on days when the news is full of the opposite. Nations still train for war, and closer to home we keep our own small weapons ready: the sharp reply, the grudge we rehearse, the silence that punishes. Into that world the prophet paints a mountain where people from everywhere come not to win but to learn. “He will teach us His ways,” they say. The Lord settles their disputes, and what was made for wounding is hammered into tools for growing food.

Isaiah does not end by telling us to wait for that day. The prophet turns to his own people: “Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the LORD.” The peace God promises for the end can begin to shape how we walk now. It might mean letting go of an old argument with a brother or sister, or taking the energy you spend defending yourself and putting it into tending something: a friendship, a meal, a neighbor’s need. We are not asked to fix the world. We can begin with one sword we are willing to hand over to be reshaped.
devotions.question: How could you hand over one sharp word, habit, or grudge to the Lord and let Him reshape it into something that helps others grow?

devotions.scriptureBody:
1 “Comfort, comfort My people,” says your God.
2 “Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her that her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned. For she has received from the hand of the LORD double for all her sins.”
3 A voice of one calling: “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert.
4 Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill made low; the uneven ground will become smooth, and the rugged land a plain.
5 And the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it.” For the mouth of the LORD has spoken.
devotions.application:
Before God says anything else, He says comfort, and He says it twice. Not to strangers, but to “My people,” people who had wandered and paid dearly for it. You may come to this passage carrying something heavy, like an apology you still haven’t managed to make to your sister. God’s first word to you is not a lecture. It is tenderness. The hard season has an end. Sin is pardoned, not merely managed.

Then a voice calls to prepare the way for the Lord. Today many churches begin Advent, the weeks of waiting and readying our hearts for Christ’s coming. Preparing a road doesn’t mean acting as if the valleys and mountains aren’t there. It means letting God reach you through them: the low places where you feel forgotten, the high places of pride or worry that block the view. The work is real, but you don’t do it alone; the God who promised that every valley shall be lifted up is the One doing the lifting. His glory will be revealed, and “all humanity together will see it.” Your part may be to clear a little space and watch for Him coming.
devotions.question: Which valley or mountain in your life most needs God’s tender word, and what small step could prepare a way for Him there?

devotions.scriptureBody:
26 In the sixth month, God sent the angel Gabriel to a town in Galilee called Nazareth,
27 to a virgin pledged in marriage to a man named Joseph, who was of the house of David. And the virgin’s name was Mary.
28 The angel appeared to her and said, “Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.”
29 Mary was greatly troubled at his words and wondered what kind of greeting this might be.
30 So the angel told her, “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.
31 Behold, you will conceive and give birth to a son, and you are to give Him the name Jesus.
32 He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David,
33 and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!”
34 “How can this be,” Mary asked the angel, “since I am a virgin?”
35 The angel replied, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God.
36 Look, even Elizabeth your relative has conceived a son in her old age, and she who was called barren is in her sixth month.
37 For no word from God will ever fail.”
38 “I am the Lord’s servant,” Mary answered. “May it happen to me according to your word.” Then the angel left her.
devotions.application:
Mary’s day probably began like any other, with chores, errands, and plans for her marriage to Joseph. Then God broke in, and her first response was not calm faith but trouble. She “wondered what kind of greeting this might be.” It is comforting that Luke tells us this. Feeling shaken when God moves isn’t failure. Her honest question, “How can this be,” meets patience, not rebuke.

Few of us will meet an angel. But we do meet moments that don’t fit our plans, like the phone call saying an aging parent can no longer live alone, and suddenly the spare room and the long evenings belong to someone else. Gabriel’s words to Mary hold for us as well: “no word from God will ever fail.” He points her to Elizabeth, a relative whose story already shows God doing the impossible. Sometimes our trust grows by looking at what God has done in someone else’s life. Mary’s answer is short and wholehearted: “I am the Lord’s servant.” She doesn’t have every detail, yet she places her plans in God’s hands. In these Advent weeks of waiting, that may be prayer enough for us too.
devotions.question: Where are unexpected circumstances unsettling your plans right now, and what might it look like to say, “I am the Lord’s servant” there?
